The deep conditioners (Mielle, tgin) and leave-ins (Shea Moisture, Aunt Jackie's, tgin) all do the same job; the 16 dollar Shea Moisture leave-in is as good as the 58 dollar salon jar for most curl types.

"A lighter skin tone is the goal of good skincare." That idea is colourism: valuing lighter skin over darker skin, even within the same family or community. Good skincare evens out marks and protects every tone; it doesn't aim to change your natural shade. Products sold to "whiten" or "bleach" skin are also where mercury, steroids and high-dose hydroquinone turn up. Safe Batch checks fade-the-mark ingredients, never lighten-the-skin ones.

"Guava leaves regrow hair and cure alopecia." Comment sections are full of personal stories, but there are no human trials. A guava leaf rinse is a safe, pleasant tradition when the leaves are used, and the bark avoided in pregnancy. Sudden shedding, bald patches (alopecia areata) or scalp eczema need a doctor; minoxidil is the proven option for thinning.

"Henna wax is henna." Non-colouring "henna wax" conditioners (like Marc Daniels) are creamy masks with a little plant extract. They won't tint hair or coat it like real henna, which is a plus if you colour your hair. Choose them for slip and moisture, not for henna's strengthening.

"High-porosity hair needs a pricey 6-step routine." A clarifying shampoo every 2 to 4 weeks, a moisturising shampoo, a rich conditioner and a leave-in cover it. Drugstore picks do the job: OGX Apple Cider Vinegar or Yves Rocher Purity for clarifying (about 13 to 22 dollars), L'Oréal Hyaluron Plump for hydrating (about 7 dollars), against 46 to 56 dollars for salon lines. Seal with an oil or butter on the ends.

"Biotin in a scalp scaler or shampoo makes hair grow." Biotin can't feed hair from the outside, and supplements only help people who are actually deficient, which is rare. Scalers clean the scalp; that's worth doing for buildup, not for growth. High-dose biotin supplements can also throw off some blood tests, so mention them to your doctor.

"Never mix vitamin C with niacinamide, or retinol with acids." Popular do/don't-mix charts mix real cautions with outdated ones. Vitamin C and niacinamide are fine together; the "they cancel out" idea came from old lab tests. Retinol with AHA or BHA isn't dangerous, just irritating for many people, so use them on different nights. Vitamin C with retinol works well split into morning and night. Check your own pair in Learn, Can I mix these?

"Use each active exactly as often as the chart says." How-often charts are a starting point. Retinoids usually start 2 to 3 nights a week, then build up to nightly if your skin is comfortable; prescription tretinoin and adapalene follow your prescriber. A benzoyl peroxide wash is often fine daily. Peels stay at once a week. Back off if skin burns, peels, or stings.

"Bikini-line bumps just need a better razor." A dermatologist's list holds up: a gentle chemical exfoliant (salicylic or glycolic) a few times a week, 10% urea cream for rough skin, fragrance-free wash, cotton underwear and loose clothes after shaving. Laser hair removal is the most effective long-term fix for ingrowns. Skip acids on freshly shaved or broken skin.

"One body scrub fixes dull skin, cellulite, ingrowns and pores." A scrub smooths texture and helps prevent ingrown hairs by clearing dead skin. It doesn't change cellulite or unclog pores beyond the surface, and it can't calm redness while it's scrubbing. Once or twice a week, then moisturize.

"Scalp scaling detoxes your scalp." Scalers (usually salicylic acid, sea salt or tea tree) lift oil, flakes and product buildup, which helps after protective styles. That's cleaning, not detox. Once a week is plenty; stop if your scalp stings or gets red.

"Layering perfume over a scented body wash and lotion makes it last." Matching scented products can help a perfume last longer, but every layer adds fragrance allergens. If you get itchy patches, use unscented lotion and spray perfume on clothes or hair ends instead. Budget dupes (like Zara's) smell similar, not identical, and are fine to try on a card first.

"Silicones are bad for your hair." For dry, bleached or damaged lengths, dimethicone and amodimethicone are some of the most useful ingredients: they reduce friction, cut breakage and protect from heat. Light buildup washes out with a regular shampoo. Skip them only if you prefer the feel without, as with silicone-free leave-ins.

"'Bond repair' rebuilds your hair from within." Most drugstore bond repair products are good conditioners with silicones, proteins and citric acid that smooth and protect. Only a few patented actives (like Olaplex's) re-link broken bonds, and mainly in bleached hair. Choose by the whole formula, not the word on the bottle.

"A hair oil with 30+ herbs is stronger than one with a few." More herbs mostly means more chances of an allergy, with each herb at a tiny dose. Look for a full ingredient list, patch test the scalp, and remember that oiling helps hair lengths, not regrowth.

"A rose toilet drop makes a cheap perfume." Toilet fresheners like Sawaday One Drop are household chemicals made for the bowl, labelled do not use near eyes and do not drink. They aren't tested on skin or hair. Use a body mist or a roll-on perfume instead.

"The right shampoo and mask make hair grow longer." Hair grows about 1 cm a month from the scalp whatever you put on the lengths. Long-hair product lists (pre-poo, shampoo, conditioner, leave-in, masks, deep conditioner) help by reducing breakage, so you keep the length you grow. A gentle shampoo, a good conditioner and low-tension styles matter more than brand. Drugstore lines like Shea Moisture, Aunt Jackie's and tgin do the same job as salon brands for many curl types.

"A body polish works as a facial scrub." Body polishes like Dove's pomegranate scrub use sugar or crushed seeds sized for legs and arms, too coarse for facial skin. Keep body scrubs below the neck and use a gentle face exfoliant, or none, on the face. Search "Stenders" in Recipes for a standalone DIY of each product in that routine, including a gentle rice and honey face polish.

"Herbal tea baths brighten and detox the skin." A tea bath is a lovely warm soak with scent and some softening from oats or milk. Herbs this dilute in a full tub don't brighten, plump, or detox. Enjoy it as relaxation, and patch test blends with mugwort, cinnamon or jasmine.

"Exfoliating shampoo plus a PDRN scalp serum stops hair shedding." Losing 50 to 100 hairs a day is normal. In this popular four-step routine, only 5% minoxidil has strong evidence. Expect extra shedding in the first 2 to 8 weeks, give it 4 to 6 months, and know that regrowth fades once you stop. Willow bark and exfoliating shampoos help flakes and an oily scalp, not regrowth. PDRN scalp serums have little evidence, and microneedle "shot" serums can prickle an irritated scalp. Sudden heavy shedding is worth a doctor visit to check iron, thyroid, or recent illness or birth. Minoxidil isn't for pregnancy or breastfeeding.

"Copper peptides or PDRN in a cleanser repair your skin." A cleanser is rinsed off within a minute, so its actives barely have time to do anything. Choose a cleanser for how gently it cleans, and spend on peptides in a leave-on serum if you want them.

"Hydrogen peroxide plus vinegar makes a peracetic acid skin treatment." It does make peracetic acid, and that's the problem: it's a strong disinfectant for hospital surfaces and food plants, corrosive to skin and eyes, and harsh to breathe. Neither ingredient belongs on skin alone, and mixed they're worse. Never mix it in a closed bottle; it can build pressure.

"A 30% AHA peel is a nightly 'look after yourself' step." AHA 30% plus BHA 2% peeling solutions are strong rinse-off peels for once a week at most, left on no longer than the label says (often 5 to 10 minutes). Not for sensitive skin, broken skin, or the same night as retinoids or scrubs. Wear sunscreen for the week after.

"'Natural' on the bottle means a natural formula." A bergamot and butterfly pea shampoo labelled "2 in 1 Natural" lists sodium laureth sulfate, sodium lauryl sulfate, two synthetic dyes and IPBC preservative near the end. That's a normal, decent shampoo, but the plants are a small part. Read the ingredient list, not the front label.

"Herbal 'bright skin' powders are gentle because they're herbal." Most are just ground herbs, but some unregistered whitening powders and creams have been found to contain mercury or steroids. Buy only ones that list their ingredients and carry a registration number (in Thailand, the อย. FDA number). Stop if skin stings, thins or lightens unevenly.

"A milky handmade toner is special because the method is secret." Frankincense extract turns water milky because resin oils cloud when they meet water. Any water-based toner sold by a small maker needs a broad-spectrum preservative and should be stability tested. Ask the seller what preserves it before you buy.

"Flaxseed gel is fine as long as it doesn't smell." Bacteria and mold can grow before there's a smell. Rinse flax masks out the same day, keep leftover gel in the fridge, and throw it out after about 3 days, or sooner if it turns cloudy or watery.

"Salt melts away swelling and heavy legs." A warm salt bath feels lovely, but salt on skin doesn't drain fluid from your legs. Moving, putting your feet up, and compression socks help. Swelling in one leg, or swelling that's new, painful or doesn't settle overnight, needs a doctor. Warming salt masks feel warm because of the salt and sugar, not because more gets into the skin.

"Dollar store skincare is too cheap to work." Price doesn't predict results; ingredients and packaging do. Budget niacinamide, hyaluronic acid and ceramide creams can be perfectly good. Be choosier with retinol and vitamin C, which break down in clear or open containers and rarely list their strength. Body creams with AHAs or kojic acid need sunscreen on exposed skin.

"An app score of 17 out of 100 means Vaseline is bad for you." Scanner apps that score products by listing every possible risk of each ingredient can give plain petroleum jelly or aloe gel a low score. Cosmetic-grade petrolatum is highly purified and one of the gentlest, most protective things for dry skin and lips. Ask why a product scored low; a number without reasons isn't a verdict.

"More acids means clearer skin." A viral five-step drugstore acne routine stacks salicylic, glycolic, and azelaic acid plus AHA, tea tree, and eucalyptus across four products. That much exfoliation strips the skin barrier and can make breakouts and dark marks worse. One exfoliating product, used a few times a week, is enough. The post's images were also labelled as AI-generated, so the products may not look or work as shown.

"Mugwort soaks fix period cramps." A warm bath can ease cramps, with or without mugwort. Mugwort is a traditional herb that's also used to bring on periods, so skip it if you could be pregnant, and if ragweed or daisy-family plants give you allergies.

"Switching products every week finds the right one faster." Most acne treatments take 6 to 12 weeks to show results, and dark marks take longer. Changing constantly also adds irritation. Add one new product at a time and give it at least 8 weeks.

"Scalp painting treats hair loss." It's a tinted pigment that hides thinning, not a treatment. Patch test 48 hours first, since hair dye allergies can be severe, and ask a doctor about the cause. Shedding after pregnancy usually recovers within about a year.

"Clean and clinically proven 8x mean a product is better." Clean has no legal definition. Claims like 8x more manageable usually come from small tests run by the brand, often compared with damaged hair and no conditioner at all.

"Brightening actives in a body scrub lighten skin." Niacinamide and arbutin need to stay on the skin to work. In a scrub they rinse away in seconds. A leave-on serum and daily sunscreen do the actual work.

"Body wraps melt fat and cellulite." Wraps pull water out of the skin for a few hours, so a thigh can measure smaller and then return. No wrap, salt, vinegar, or mustard breaks down fat, and wraps that burn or tingle are damaging the skin.

"Cinnamon and clove make every product more natural." Cinnamon bark and clove oils are among the most common causes of skin allergy. Kept on the scalp, in a bath, or in a leave-in, they can burn. Leave them out, or use a tiny amount only in rinse-off products.

"Charcoal shampoo detoxes the scalp and black soybean stops hair loss." Charcoal in a wash-off product rinses away in seconds and doesn't remove toxins. There's no good evidence that soybean in shampoo prevents hair loss; for thinning, minoxidil is the proven option.
"Flaxseed gel removes toxins." The digestive benefits people describe come from eating flaxseed. On skin and hair it's a slippery gel that defines curls, and it spoils within days.

"Menthol is all-natural, so a lot of it is fine." Menthol does come from mint, but it works by triggering cold receptors, and too much burns and stings. Keep it near 1% in soap and body wash and at 5% or less in balms, keep it away from children under 6, and remember that borneol is a different, camphor-like compound that's toxic if swallowed.

"Coffee tightens skin, prevents aging, and fades acne marks." Caffeine briefly narrows blood vessels, so skin can look a little tighter for a few hours. That doesn't prevent aging (daily sunscreen does), and scrubbing inflamed spots tends to make marks worse, not better.
"You can shave with a sugar scrub." Grains trapped under a razor cause nicks and razor burn. Scrub, rinse, then shave over a proper lather or gel, and skip the scrub on freshly shaved skin.

"Rose hydrosol in the lye water makes the soap smell like roses." Lye breaks down delicate floral scents, so almost none of the hydrosol's smell survives. Scent comes from essential oils or fragrance added at trace.

"Chamomile and calendula soap soothes sensitive skin." Any true soap is alkaline, and most of the herbs' benefit doesn't survive the lye. A gentle soap is fine for many people, but very sensitive or eczema-prone skin usually does better with a soap-free cleanser.
"Collagen boost oil firms skin." The card itself admits oils don't create new collagen. Retinoids and daily sunscreen are what protect collagen.
"Butterfly pea gel prevents greying and grows hair." There's no good evidence for either. It's a pretty blue gel; with water and fresh aloe it also spoils in days.
"Almond oil and turmeric lighten a dark bikini line." Darkening there comes from friction, shaving, and hormones. Gentler hair removal and less rubbing help; turmeric only stains.
"Toilet bombs are a skin DIY." They're a cleaning product. Keep citric acid cleaners away from bleach, and store them away from children.
"Tangerine fades stretch marks and grapefruit brightens skin." Citrus oils in a body oil add scent. They don't fade marks, and expressed grapefruit oil can cause sun reactions on skin.

"Skin So Soft keeps bugs away." Citronella and lavender repel mosquitoes for only a short time, often under an hour. For real protection, use a repellent with icaridin (picaridin) or DEET, as Health Canada recommends.
"Homemade perfume is chemical-free." Essential oils are mixtures of strong chemicals, and some are common skin allergens. Keep perfume oils to about 3 to 5% in a carrier, and patch test.
"Frankincense, myrrh, and sandalwood are better than Botox." No essential oil relaxes muscles or lifts sagging skin. They're pleasant scents in a moisturizer, used at about 1% or less.

"Liquid Morphine roller blend relieves pain like a painkiller." The name is marketing. Massage and a cooling scent can feel nice, but 60 drops in a 10 ml roller is about 30% essential oil, roughly 15 times the safe amount for skin.

"Beeswax and olive oil make homemade Vaseline." It's a lovely balm, but it isn't petroleum jelly and doesn't behave the same way. Don't put essential oils like eucalyptus or peppermint in a balm for babies or young children.

"Postpartum herbal sprays and balms heal tears and stitches." Perineal sprays and sitz baths can soothe, but healing stitches need your provider's guidance. Avoid strong essential oils down there, and get any heat, smell, or worsening pain checked.

"Castile soap diluted with water keeps for weeks." Undiluted castile is alkaline enough to resist germs, but once you add water, aloe, milk, or rose water, it becomes a place for bacteria to grow. Dilute only what you'll use in a few days, or skip the water.

"Add glycolic or lactic acid to castile soap for a peeling body wash." Acid and real soap cancel each other out; the soap turns cloudy and greasy and the acid stops working. AHA washes need synthetic, acid-friendly cleansers.

"An antifungal soap clears under-breast rash." Keeping the area clean and dry helps, but a fungal rash usually needs an antifungal cream. If it doesn't improve in a week or two, see a pharmacist or doctor.
"Prickly pear, plum kernel, or mongongo oil protects against UV." No plant oil is a sunscreen. Their sun protection is tiny and untested; use a tested broad-spectrum sunscreen.
"Cacay oil is a natural source of retinoic acid." All-trans retinoic acid is tretinoin, a prescription drug. Cacay oil has only traces of vitamin A compounds; it's a nice light oil, not a retinoid.
"Açaí oil on skin aids weight loss, diabetes, and heart health." Those claims come from eating the fruit, and even then they're weak. A skin oil only moisturizes.
"Toner tab water keeps a week in the fridge." Water with plant bits and no preservative grows bacteria within days, fridge or not. Use it the same day.

"Murumuru, kokum, and bacuri butters treat eczema, boost collagen, and fight viruses." Exotic butters are lovely moisturizers, and that's what the evidence supports. Lists claiming antiviral, collagen-boosting, or arthritis-relieving powers come from sellers, not studies.
"Magnesium lotion helps you sleep and stops cramps." Very little magnesium gets through skin, and studies haven't shown it fixes cramps or sleep. The massage and routine may still feel relaxing.
"Slimming body butter melts fat." No essential oil blend rubbed on skin burns fat or slims you. Citrus blends like Slim & Sassy can also cause sun reactions on skin.

"This soap cleared my baby's severe eczema." Testimonials aren't evidence. A gentle, fragrance-free soap can avoid making eczema worse, but it can't heal it. Severe eczema, especially in babies, needs a doctor's care.
"Cocoa butter fades stretch marks and scars." Studies of cocoa butter found it didn't prevent or fade stretch marks. It's a lovely moisturizer, and that's the honest claim.
"An essential oil butter supports your immune system." Rubbing scented butter on skin doesn't change your immune system. Enjoy it as a moisturizer.

"Butters and helichrysum erase scars." Keeping a healed scar moisturized can make it feel softer, and silicone gel sheets have the best evidence. No oil blend removes a scar, and nothing goes on an open wound.

"Beeswax emulsifies water into a cream." Beeswax thickens oils but can't hold water in for long. Creams made with only beeswax separate, and any cream with water needs a real emulsifier and a preservative, even in the fridge.
"A long cure fixes a lye-heavy soap." Curing lets water evaporate and the bar harden. If a recipe has more lye than its oils can use, the extra lye stays in the bar. Get the lye right on paper first.

"Potassium and sodium hydroxide are interchangeable." Potassium hydroxide (KOH) makes soft or liquid soap like savon noir; sodium hydroxide (NaOH) makes hard bars. They're needed in different amounts (about 1.4 g of KOH for every 1 g of NaOH), so never swap one for the other gram for gram.
"Tummy tuck cream tightens your stomach." No essential oil blend in a lotion can tighten skin or burn fat. It's a scented moisturizer.

"Sodium hydroxide on a soap label means lye is left in the bar." Labels list what went in. In a properly made soap, all the lye reacts with the oils and turns into soap (sodium olivate, sodium cocoate) and glycerin; none is left over.

"Aleppo soap should be green all the way through, or it's bad quality." Real Aleppo soap is aged for months, and the outside turns tan or brown while the inside stays green. A brown surface is normal aging.

"Savon noir for cleaning windows is the same as Moroccan black soap for the hammam." French savon noir is a concentrated household soap for floors and windows. Moroccan beldi soap is made for skin. Don't swap one for the other.
"Put a healing salve on a fresh burn." Oil and wax hold heat in. Cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes first; salves are for later, once the skin has closed.
"Turmeric tablets in the bath give glowing skin." Supplements are made to be swallowed. In a bath they mostly stain the tub, towels, and skin yellow.

"Garlic in olive oil grows nails overnight." Raw garlic can burn the skin around your nails, and garlic left sitting in oil can grow botulism. Plain oil or a cuticle oil massaged in nightly does the real work.

"Grated potato, rice flour, and honey set into a soap." Without a soap base or lye, nothing in it cleans or sets, and fresh potato juice spoils within a day. Stir rice flour into melt-and-pour base instead.

"Optional oils in a lye recipe can just be left out." Every oil uses up part of the lye. Leave one out without lowering the lye and the bar can turn caustic. Re-run the recipe through a soap calculator whenever you change the oils.

"Glutathione powder in a body cream lightens skin." There's little evidence glutathione rubbed on skin changes its color, and unlabeled "Snow White" powders sold online have been found with mercury or steroids. Leave them out of anything you make.

"Kyphi and attar are skin perfumes." Kyphi is incense, made to be burned, not rubbed on skin. A traditional attar is a tiny amount of scent in a carrier; 2 tablespoons of pure sandalwood essential oil on skin is far too strong.

"Aloe vera and a vitamin C tablet make a natural sunscreen." Neither has any SPF, and crushed vitamin C tablets can sting. A gel like this gives zero protection while making you feel protected. Use a tested sunscreen.

"Garlic and cloves steeped in oil for days grow hair." There's no good evidence garlic grows hair, and fresh garlic sitting in oil is a botulism risk. Dried rosemary or plain oils are the safer route.

"You can make skin-lightening products at home." Real lightening ingredients like hydroquinone, tranexamic acid, and hexylresorcinol are drugs or lab-made actives that need exact dosing; hydroquinone isn't allowed in cosmetics in Canada. At home, stick to gentle brightening (exfoliation) and daily sunscreen.

"Breast oil moves lymph and prevents disease." A massage oil feels nice and helps you notice changes in your body, which is genuinely useful. It doesn't detox or prevent breast disease, and any new lump needs a doctor.

"Mix rice flour, honey, and coconut oil, pour it in a mold, and you have soap." Without a soap base or lye there's nothing in it that cleans or sets. You get a soft paste. Stir the powders into melted melt-and-pour base instead.
"Melt-and-pour soap needs to cure for 2 to 4 weeks." Curing is for lye soap made from scratch. Melt-and-pour is ready as soon as it's hard; wrap it so it doesn't "sweat".

"The dukhan smoke bath detoxes skin." Smoke doesn't remove toxins; the glow comes from heat and the wood's oils and resin settling on skin. Sitting over hot coals can burn you, and in a closed room the smoke can cause carbon monoxide poisoning. Keep a window open, keep a gap from the coals, and skip it in pregnancy or if you have asthma.

"Adding fresh herbs to oil and sun-infusing it for weeks makes it stronger." Fresh aloe, onion, cactus, or leaves carry water into the oil, and warm jars left for weeks are where mold and bacteria thrive. Use fully dried herbs, infuse once, strain well, and the oil keeps for months.
"Pumpkin seed oil on the scalp blocks DHT." The small studies behind this used capsules taken by mouth, not oil rubbed on the scalp. As a hair oil it conditions; it isn't a hair loss treatment.

"New mothers shouldn't bathe for weeks." Warm baths and showers are safe and help hygiene after birth. Keep warm afterwards if that's comforting, and follow your provider's advice about soaking after stitches or a C-section.
"Manjistha or mulethi soap whitens skin and cures acne." In a rinse-off bar these mainly add color. A soap can't change your skin tone, and persistent acne needs proper treatment.

"Wood ash soap is chemical-free and gentler." Soaking ash makes potassium lye, the same kind of caustic chemical as store-bought lye, but you can't tell how strong it is. pH strips read about 13 whether it's weak or dangerously strong, so you can't work out how much oil it needs. Bars can come out caustic. Measured store-bought lye with a soap calculator is the safer route.

"Fruit soap gives fair skin." Fresh papaya, pineapple, and lemon juice spoil inside melt-and-pour, and a rinse-off bar can't change your skin tone. Daily sunscreen does more for even tone than any soap.
"Silk protein soap improves skin elasticity." Silk protein makes lather feel silkier. Nothing in a rinse-off bar changes skin elasticity.
"Grape or cucumber in soap fights wrinkles." Fresh fruit juice in soap mostly adds color, and it can spoil the bar. Antioxidants rinsed off in seconds can't affect wrinkles.
"Walnut scrubs remove tan." Crushed walnut shells have sharp edges that can scratch skin. Fine sugar or a gentle acid exfoliant is kinder, and tan fades on its own.
"Coffee scrubs reduce cellulite." Caffeine can make skin look slightly tighter for a few hours. Cellulite is a structure under the skin that no scrub changes.

"Snow-white powder and serum whiten skin safely." Unlabeled "whitening" powders and serums sold online have been found to contain mercury or strong steroids. Don't use any skin product without a full ingredient list.
"Oil blends firm and tone skin." Oils make skin look smoother and more supple while they're on it. They can't tighten loose skin or reduce cellulite.
"Ubtan removes tan." Ubtan powders gently exfoliate, so skin can look brighter for a day or two. Tan fades on its own as skin renews over weeks, and sunscreen is what prevents it.
"Honey adds moisture to a balm." Honey doesn't dissolve in oils and butters. In a balm it sinks or forms sticky beads unless you add an emulsifier.

"Honey and cinnamon release peroxide that bleaches body hair." Honey makes only tiny amounts of peroxide, far too little to lift hair color, and cinnamon doesn't make any. Cinnamon is a common cause of skin burns, especially under plastic wrap.

"Natural lighteners have zero risk of irritation." Lemon juice can blister skin in sunlight, and cinnamon causes burning rashes. Plain 3% peroxide, rinsed off after 15 minutes, is often gentler than these "natural" mixes.

"Zinc oxide and carrot seed oil make a natural sunscreen." Carrot seed oil has no SPF. Zinc only protects when it's spread evenly at a tested strength, and a home blend clumps, so you can't know how much protection you're getting. It's no substitute for a tested sunscreen.
"Deodorant cream brightens underarms." Darker underarms usually come from friction, shaving irritation, or hormones. Gentler hair removal and less rubbing help more than any deodorant.
"Selling DIY scrubs is easy money." In Canada and the US, anything you sell as a cosmetic must be labeled correctly, and in Canada it must be reported to Health Canada within 10 days of first sale.
"Kojic acid soap whitens skin." Kojic acid breaks down in fresh lye soap and darkens over time, and a rinse-off bar touches skin for seconds. Daily sunscreen does more for dark spots than any soap.
"Vinegar and castile soap make a balanced shampoo." The acid and the soap neutralize each other into a cloudy, greasy mix. Use them one after the other, never in the same bottle.

"Never touch clay with a metal spoon." A quick stir with a stainless steel spoon doesn't change clay in any way you'd notice. The real rule on that same advice is the useful one: mix clay with water just before using it, and don't store it wet.
"Lime or lemon juice in soap adds vitamin C." Lye destroys vitamin C, and the citric acid in the juice uses up a little of the lye. It changes the lye math rather than adding a skin benefit.
"Eucalyptus soap clears congestion." The scent can feel refreshing in a steamy shower, but a rinse-off soap has too little time and scent to treat a stuffy nose. It isn't a treatment for a cold.
"Purple Brazilian clay detoxifies your skin." Clays soak up surface oil and dirt, and that's useful. They don't pull toxins out of skin; your liver and kidneys do that job.

"Natural soap is chemical-free." Every real bar soap is made with lye, and every ingredient is a chemical. What matters is whether the recipe's lye amount is right, which the soap lye check works out.
"Soap brightens skin and evens tone." Soap is on your skin for under a minute before it's rinsed off. Turmeric, licorice, or rice in a bar can't do much in that time.

"Castile soap makes a gentle shampoo." Castile soap is alkaline, around pH 9 to 10. On hair it can leave a dull, tangly film, especially with hard water. A melt-and-pour shampoo base or a mild store shampoo is gentler.

"Lemon juice and sunlight gently lighten body hair." Lemon or lime juice on skin in the sun can cause phytophotodermatitis: burns and dark streaks that last months. Chamomile on its own lightens little. Lighten hair indoors with a product made for it, or skip it.
"Perfume oil is 80 to 90% essential oils." That's far too strong for skin. Roll-on perfume oils should be mostly carrier oil, with essential oils around 3 to 5% at most.
"Beeswax turns water and oil into a cream." Beeswax thickens oils, but it isn't an emulsifier. Creams need an emulsifying wax and a preservative.
"Caffeine erases dark circles." It can briefly reduce puffiness. Dark circles from pigment, thin skin, or genetics don't change.

"Castor oil grows longer, thicker lashes." Castor oil conditions lashes and may reduce breakage, but no study shows it grows new hair. Prescription bimatoprost is the only proven lash growth treatment.
"Homemade kajal is safe for eyes." Lamp soot isn't purified, and homemade eye products aren't sterile. Eye infections and irritation are real risks.
"Store mascara is full of chemicals; homemade is safer." Store mascara has preservatives and film formers so it doesn't grow bacteria in a damp tube. Homemade versions lack both.
"DIY collagen serums and blush boost collagen." Collagen applied to skin can't get in to build more. Mica blush adds color, not collagen.
"Facial hair removal dough removes hair." Rubbing a dried besan paste can pull out some fine, soft hair, but not coarse hair, and over-rubbing irritates. The post's own note says it isn't permanent.
"Lemon and turmeric fix dark underarms." Underarm darkening usually comes from friction, shaving, or deodorant irritation. Lemon juice can irritate and darken it further.
"Glycerin fights acne and evens skin tone." Glycerin is an excellent humectant that hydrates skin. It isn't an acne treatment or a brightener.
"Beetroot makes lips pink." It stains them temporarily, like a tint. It doesn't change lip color.

"Alum and glycerin make a soap that clears acne." Alum dissolved in water and glycerin stays liquid; it won't set into a bar, and it has nothing that cleanses. The before-and-after photos on these posts aren't evidence.
"This recipe is a 1% dilution." Check the math: about 20 drops make 1 ml. So 21 drops in 2 oz (about 60 ml) is roughly 1.75%, not 1%. The checker counts drops for you.
"Coconut essential oil." There isn't one. Coconut-scented products use fragrance oil.
"Natural deodorant stops sweat." Deodorants only mask odor. Only aluminum-based antiperspirants reduce sweating.
"Detox baths draw out toxins." Salt, clay, and spirulina don't pull toxins through skin. A warm bath is relaxing, and that's the real benefit.
"Herbal bath tea relieves cold and flu." Warm steam can feel soothing for a stuffy nose, but it doesn't treat an infection.
"Add lemon to baking soda for whiter teeth." Baking soda can lift surface stains, but lemon juice is acidic and wears away enamel permanently.
"Coconut oil aids digestion and weight loss." Rubbing it on skin does neither, and eating it adds a lot of saturated fat.
"Simmer fresh aloe or carrots in oil." Cooking doesn't remove all the water. Oils made with fresh produce can grow mold within days.
"Lemon essential oil exfoliates and fades age spots." It doesn't exfoliate at all, and cold-pressed lemon oil causes burns and dark patches in sunlight.

"Sea moss supports thyroid, fertility, and works like Botox." Iodine content varies hugely between batches, and too much iodine can upset the thyroid. Some samples contain heavy metals. Ask a doctor before taking it, especially with a thyroid condition.
"Herbs balance hormones and treat PCOS." Vitex can interact with birth control and fertility treatment. PCOS needs a doctor's care; herbs aren't a substitute.
"Dermarolling improves results by 70%." There's no basis for that number. Home microneedling risks infection and scarring, especially over oils that aren't sterile.
"Make your own sunscreen with zinc oxide." Homemade sunscreen can't be tested and usually protects far less than expected. Buy a tested SPF 30 or higher.
"Ice cubes shrink pores." Cold makes skin look tighter for a few minutes. Pore size doesn't change.
"Coconut oil heals wounds and scars." Keeping a healing wound moist helps, but petroleum jelly does it better, and no oil removes scars.
"Smells like a designer perfume." Designer perfumes use dozens of ingredients, including synthetic ones. A three-oil blend can be pleasant, but it won't smell like a specific brand.
"Natural means safe." Poison ivy is natural. Plant chemicals are some of the most common causes of skin allergies.
"Vitamin E is a preservative." It only slows oils going rancid. It does nothing against bacteria or mold.
"Grapefruit seed extract preserves naturally." Lab tests found its effect came from synthetic preservatives added during processing.
"If it tingles, it's working." Tingling, stinging, or burning is irritation. Rinse it off.
"The fridge keeps it safe." Cold slows microbes; it doesn't stop them. Water-based DIYs still spoil within days.
"Steam opens pores." Pores have no muscles, so they don't open or close. Steam softens oil and dead skin, which is why cleansing afterward feels easier.
"Y, O, and U shaped pores." This isn't a dermatology classification. Pore size comes mostly from genetics, oil, age, and sun damage, and no ingredient permanently shrinks pores.
"Clay draws out toxins." Clay soaks up oil and surface grime. Your liver and kidneys handle toxins.
"Fuller's earth treats sunburn." Drying clay on burned skin makes it worse. Use cool water and plain aloe gel, and see a doctor for blistering.
"Rice water grows longer, stronger hair." There's no good evidence it speeds growth. It can make hair feel smoother, but left in, it leaves hair stiff and dry.
"Breast tightening oil." Breasts are held up by ligaments and fat under the skin. Oils only moisturize the surface; no oil firms or lifts.
"Castor oil or aloe fades stretch marks." Nothing applied at home reliably removes stretch marks. Moisturizing can make them less itchy while they're new.
"Vitamin E heals scars." Studies found it doesn't improve scars, and it causes rashes in some people.
"Onion juice regrows hair." The evidence is one small study in people with patchy hair loss (alopecia areata). It doesn't treat ordinary thinning, and it can irritate the scalp.
"Curry leaf water prevents grey hair." Greying is mostly genetic. There's no good evidence that any rinse delays it.
"Keeps 1 week in the fridge." Unpreserved water-based mixes can grow bacteria within days even when chilled. Three days is a safer limit.
"Collagen gels." Plants don't contain collagen, and collagen molecules are too big to soak into skin. Okra, flax, and rice gels are slippery, hydrating gels and nothing more.
"Rinse with cool water to close pores." Water temperature doesn't change pores. Hot water does dry skin out, so lukewarm is best.
"Epsom salt soaks give you magnesium." Skin absorbs very little. The warm water is what helps.
"Essential oils are full of vitamins and omega fatty acids." They contain neither. Those come from carrier oils like rosehip or argan.
Before-and-after photos. Many of these posts use AI-generated or edited pictures. Hair grows about 1 cm a month, so no oil turns short grey hair into a 90 cm black braid in 4 weeks.
"Fix dark knees in 7 days." Darker knees usually come from friction and genetics and fade slowly, if at all. The lemon juice step in these plans can make the darkening worse.

"Perfume tea makes you smell good." There's no evidence that drinking herbal tea changes body odor. If you drink star anise tea, buy it from a food seller: Japanese star anise is toxic and has been found mixed into Chinese star anise.
"Coconut, olive, and macadamia oil have natural SPF." Oils block almost no UV, far too little to protect skin or hair. Relying on them leads to sunburn. Use a real sunscreen.
"Nettle and saw palmetto block DHT." The hair studies used pills, mostly in men. There's little evidence that rubbing them on the scalp does the same.
"Rosemary oil works like minoxidil." This comes from one small 2015 study. It's promising but far from proven, and rosemary oil still needs diluting.

"Teas for hair growth." There's no good evidence that drinking any of these teas grows hair. Hair loss with a sudden change is worth a doctor's visit, since iron, thyroid, and hormone problems are common causes.
"Horsetail's silica strengthens hair." This isn't backed by good studies. Drinking horsetail long-term can also deplete vitamin B1.
"Yoni oil balances pH and hormones." The vagina regulates its own pH, and oils on the vulva don't affect hormones. Itching or odor usually needs a diagnosis, not an oil.
"Batana oil regrows hair." There are no studies showing this. It's a rich conditioning oil.
"Herbal toothpaste replaces fluoride." Fluoride is what prevents cavities. Herbal pastes can freshen breath, but use them alongside a fluoride toothpaste.

"A neem sitz bath treats vaginal infections." Warm water can soothe itching, but yeast infections and bacterial vaginosis need a diagnosis and proper treatment. The poster is right about one thing: never douche.
"Oils fade dark knees, elbows, and scars." Moisturizing softens rough skin, but no oil reliably lightens dark patches or removes scars.
"Lemon peel extract for pores." Lemon and lime peel contain the compounds that cause sun burns and dark patches. Skip them in DIYs.
"Oils lift and tighten saggy skin." Sagging comes from lost collagen and elastin under the skin. Oils moisturize the surface but can't firm, tone, or lift, and mustard oil can irritate.

"Cinnamon water detoxifies and clears blemishes." Your liver and kidneys do the detoxing. The poster is right to say Ceylon cinnamon: common cassia cinnamon has coumarin, which can harm the liver if you drink it daily in large amounts.
"Brightening scrubs lighten inner thighs, knees, and elbows." Darkening there usually comes from friction and genetics. Scrubbing harder adds friction, which can make it darker.
"Infuse oil in the sun for 7 days." Heat and UV light make oils go rancid faster. A warm, dark cupboard or a gentle double boiler works better.
"Oregano oil for hair growth." Oregano essential oil is one of the most irritating oils on skin, and there's no good evidence it grows hair. Dried oregano in an infused oil is milder.
